prompt.context: This section contains four brain teasers commonly used in consulting interviews. Each tests spatial reasoning, estimation, or logical problem-solving.
prompt.question: Answer each of the following brain teasers: (1) Calendar Cube: You have two cubes with 6 sides each (12 sides total). You want to display all days of the month (01 through 31) using these two cubes. What digits do you put on each cube? (2) Chopped Cube: You have a large cube made up of small cubes, where each side of the large cube is 10 small cubes wide. How many small cubes make up the outside of the large cube? (3) Ping-Pong Balls in a 747: How many ping-pong balls can you fit in a Boeing 747 airplane? (4) JFK Airport: How many people fly in and out of JFK every day?

clarifying_info.q: For the calendar cube, can a digit appear on both cubes?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, a digit can appear on both cubes if needed.

clarifying_info.q: For the calendar cube, can a face be flipped/reused as another digit?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, a face can be flipped — for example a 6 can also serve as a 9.

clarifying_info.q: For the ping-pong ball question, does the plane have seats installed?
clarifying_info.a: You can ask and make an assumption — either way is acceptable; state your assumption.

clarifying_info.q: For JFK, is the question about arrivals, departures, or both?
clarifying_info.a: Both arrivals and departures (total passengers passing through).

framework: Spatial/logic puzzles: Draw or enumerate systematically, use constraints to narrow down
Estimation questions: Break into components (volume, rate, density), state assumptions explicitly, keep numbers round and easy to compute
Sanity-check answers against intuition; adjust packing/waste factors as needed
Show structured thinking out loud; questioning the underlying premise adds bonus points

questions.prompt: Calendar Cube: What digits go on each cube?
questions.guidance: The key constraint is that both cubes must be used together to show any date from 01 to 31. Every digit 0-9 must be reachable. The trick is that 12 sides cannot hold all 10 distinct digits on two separate cubes without overlap, so both cubes need 0 and 1 (to form 01-09 and 10-19). The insight is that 6 can be flipped upside down to serve as 9, eliminating the need for a separate 9 face.

math.setup: Cube 1 must have: 0,1,2,3,4,5 (to combine with Cube 2 for dates in the teens and single-digits). Cube 2 must have: 0,1,2,6,7,8 (6 doubles as 9). Verify all dates 01-31 are achievable: 01(C2=0,C1=1), 02(C2=0,C1=2),...,09(C2=0,C1=6flipped), 10(C1=1,C2=0), 11(C1=1,C2=1 — both cubes have 1), 12(C1=1,C2=2),...,19(C1=1,C2=6flipped), 20(C2=2,C1=0), 21(C2=2,C1=1),...,29(C2=2,C1=6flipped), 30(C2=3,C1=0 — Cube 1 has 3), 31(C2=3,C1=1).
steps: Both cubes share 0, 1, 2 to handle 11, 22, and flexible single-digit pairings
6 on Cube 2 serves double duty as 9 when flipped

questions.prompt: Chopped Cube: How many small cubes make up the outside surface of a 10x10x10 large cube?
questions.guidance: Avoid the trap of counting 10x10x6 = 600 (this double-counts edges and corners). The clean approach is to remove two opposing faces and count the remaining four faces as rectangles that exclude already-counted edges.

math.setup: Large cube is 10x10x10 small cubes. Count only the outer shell.
steps: Remove those two faces; remaining four faces each measure 10 wide x 8 deep (excluding the two already-counted face layers) = 10x8 = 80... wait — correct approach: four sides each 10x10 but they share edges with the removed faces. Use the subtraction method: four remaining faces each = 9 wide x 10 tall = 90? Re-derive cleanly: total = 10^3 - 8^3 = 1000 - 512 = 488

questions.prompt: Ping-Pong Balls in a 747: How many fit?
questions.guidance: Treat the 747 as a cylinder to approximate its volume. Estimate a ping-pong ball as a 1-inch diameter sphere. Divide volumes and apply a packing efficiency factor (~75% for random packing, meaning ~25% is wasted space). Bonus: question the premise — could you ship a ball-making machine instead?

math.setup: Approximate 747 as cylinder: length = 200 feet, diameter = 20 feet, radius = 10 feet. Ping-pong ball diameter = 1 inch = 1/12 foot, radius = 1/24 foot.
steps: Volume of 747 cylinder: π × r² × l = π × 100 × 200 ≈ 3.14 × 20,000 ≈ 62,800 cubic feet
Convert to cubic inches: 62,800 × 12³ = 62,800 × 1,728 ≈ 108,518,400 cubic inches
Volume of one ping-pong ball (sphere, r=0.5 in): (4/3)π r³ = (4/3) × 3.14 × 0.125 ≈ 0.524 cubic inches
math.answer: Approximately 150–200 million ping-pong balls (order of magnitude: ~10^8)

questions.prompt: JFK Airport: How many passengers fly in and out per day?
questions.guidance: Break it down: number of runways → planes per day → passengers per plane. Apply realistic operating hours (planes don't fly between ~11pm and 5am). State each assumption clearly and keep arithmetic simple.

math.setup: JFK has 5 runways. Planes arrive/depart every 15 minutes per runway. Airport operates ~18 hours per day (5am to 11pm).
steps: Planes per runway per day: 4 × 18 = 72... use simplified: 4 per hour × 18 hours = 72, but casebook uses 4 per hour concept differently
Casebook approach: 5 runways × 18 hours × 4 planes/hr = 360 planes/day
math.answer: ~72,000 passengers per day; ~26 million per year

brainstorming.prompt: For the ping-pong ball question, what are additional considerations or creative angles a candidate could raise?

categories.name: Refinements to the estimate
ideas: Adjust for seats and cabin equipment reducing usable volume
Account for wing fuel tanks (could add volume if emptied)
Use tighter sphere packing models (face-centered cubic ~74% efficiency)

categories.name: Questioning the premise
ideas: Why are we filling a 747 with ping-pong balls? What is the business purpose?
Could raw plastic pellets and a ball-manufacturing machine ship more balls to destination?
Is weight a binding constraint before volume?

categories.name: Clarifying assumptions
ideas: Are seats removed or in place?
What size ping-pong ball — standard 40mm tournament or practice balls?

recommendation: Brain teasers reward structured decomposition over raw computation
Always state assumptions out loud and check the answer for reasonableness
For spatial puzzles, use systematic enumeration or algebraic shortcuts (e.g., total minus interior)
risks: Rushing to arithmetic without framing the approach
Missing elegant tricks (e.g., 6-as-9 flip in the calendar cube)
Forgetting packing efficiency in volume estimation questions
next_steps: Verify answers by checking edge cases (e.g., confirm all 31 dates work for the calendar cube)
For estimation, always sanity-check the final number against real-world knowledge
